rows.answer: The Transformer achieved a BLEU score of 28.4 on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task [1][3].
The Transformer achieved a BLEU score of 41.0 on the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task [1][2]. The document states that the model was trained for 3.5 days on eight GPUs [3].
The Transformer encoder stack is composed of N = 6 identical layers. [1]
The Transformer employs h = 8 parallel attention heads, with each head using dimensions dk = dv = dmodel/h = 64 [2].
The Transformer learning rate schedule used 4,000 warmup steps [1].
The Transformer models were trained on one machine equipped with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs [10].
The base Transformer models were trained for a total of 100,000 steps, which took 12 hours [1][2].
The Transformer authors used a label smoothing value of 0.1 [1]. This technique hurt perplexity by making the model more unsure, but it improved both accuracy and the BLEU score [1].

The Transformer uses sine and cosine functions of different frequencies for its positional encodings [1]. Specifically, the positional encoding is defined by the formulas PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos/10000^(2i/dmodel)) and PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos/10000^(2i/dmodel)) [1]. The authors chose this sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those encountered during training [4].

The per-layer computational complexity of a self-attention layer is O(n² · d), whereas a recurrent layer has a complexity of O(n · d²) [3]. Self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when the sequence length n is less than the representation dimension d [1].
BERTBASE contains 110M parameters and BERTLARGE contains 340M parameters [1][3].
BERT masks 15% of all WordPiece tokens in each sequence at random during pre-training [1][3].

When BERT selects a token for masked prediction, it replaces the token with the [MASK] token 80% of the time, a random token 10% of the time, or leaves the token unchanged 10% of the time [1]. This specific distribution is also detailed in the ablation studies as 80% MASK, 10% SAME, and 10% RND [8].

BERTLARGE obtained a score of 80.5 on the official GLUE leaderboard [1][3]. Additionally, BERTBASE and BERTLARGE achieved average accuracy improvements of 4.5% and 7.0% respectively over the prior state of the art [3].
BERT reached a Test F1 of 93.2 on SQuAD v1.1 [1][4].
BERT reached a Test F1 of 83.1 on SQuAD v2.0 [1][2].
BERT was pre-trained on the BooksCorpus, which contains 800 million words, and English Wikipedia, which contains 2,500 million words [1][4].
In BERT's next sentence prediction task, 50% of the time sentence B is the actual next sentence that follows sentence A, and 50% of the time it is a random sentence from the corpus [1][7].
BERT uses a WordPiece vocabulary of 30,000 tokens [1].
BERT was pre-trained for 1,000,000 steps with a batch size of 128,000 words [2].
With BERT, finding the most similar pair among 10,000 sentences takes about 65 hours, whereas with SBERT it takes about 5 seconds [1][3][5].

Sentence-BERT uses siamese and triplet network structures to derive semantically meaningful sentence embeddings [1][2]. These structures are applied to fine-tune the pretrained BERT or RoBERTa networks [2][9].

Sentence-BERT experiments with three pooling strategies: using the output of the CLS-token, computing the mean of all output vectors (MEAN strategy), and computing a max-over-time of the output vectors (MAX strategy) [1].
The default pooling strategy in SBERT is MEAN. [1][2][3]
The SNLI dataset contains 570,000 sentence pairs, while the MultiNLI dataset contains 430,000 sentence pairs [1].
To fine-tune SBERT on NLI data, a batch size of 16, the Adam optimizer, and a learning rate of 2e−5 were used [1].
In SBERT's triplet objective, the Euclidean distance is used as the metric, and the margin ϵ is set to 1. [1]

The smart batching strategy in SBERT groups sentences with similar lengths together and pads them only to the longest element within a mini-batch [1]. This approach drastically reduces the computational overhead associated with padding tokens [1].
SBERT can be fine-tuned in less than 20 minutes [1].

The Sentence-BERT paper evaluates argument similarity on the Argument Facet Similarity (AFS) corpus [2][3]. This corpus contains 6,000 annotated sentential argument pairs from social media dialogs on topics such as gun control, gay marriage, and the death penalty [2].

The Dense Passage Retriever outperforms BM25 by 9% to 19% absolute in terms of top-20 passage retrieval accuracy [1]. For example, on the Natural Questions dataset, the top-20 accuracy is 78.4% for DPR compared to 59.1% for BM25 [6][8].

The documents do not specify the exact length of the passages, only noting that they are split into "equal lengths" and that fixed-length passages perform better than natural paragraphs [2][10]. The total number of passages, denoted as M, can be very large, with the specific experiments described in the paper using 21 million passages [1].

The documents indicate that the RAG paper used the December 2018 Wikipedia dump, splitting articles into disjoint 100-word chunks to create a total of 21 million documents [1]. Similarly, the Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) paper utilized the English Wikipedia dump from December 20, 2018, as its source for answering questions [2]. While the Self-RAG paper primarily used 2018 English Wikipedia embeddings, it switched to a December 2020 preprocessed corpus for the PopQA dataset to address missing recent entities [4].

DPR measures similarity by applying a dot product to the d-dimensional vectors of the question and the passage, defined as sim(q, p) = EQ(q)⊺EP(p) [1]. This decomposable similarity function allows the passage representations to be precomputed, and the system retrieves the k passages with vectors closest to the question vector [1]. While other decomposable functions like cosine and Euclidean L2 distance exist, the paper notes that L2 performs comparably to dot product, and both are superior to cosine [2].

The retrieval component in RAG is based on DPR, which follows a bi-encoder architecture [2]. At run-time, DPR uses a different encoder to map the input question to a vector and retrieves passages whose vectors are closest to the question vector [1]. The similarity between the question and passage is defined using the dot product of their vectors [1].
The main DPR model was trained with a batch size of 128, using in-batch negative settings that included one additional BM25 negative passage per question [1].
DPR trained using only 1,000 examples already outperforms BM25 [2][3].
DPR can process 995.0 questions per second at run time [1].
Computing dense embeddings for 21 million passages takes roughly 8.8 hours on 8 GPUs [1].

BM25 performs better than DPR on SQuAD because the questions were written by annotators after seeing the passages, resulting in high lexical overlap that favors BM25's keyword matching [2]. Additionally, the SQuAD data was collected from a limited set of over 500 Wikipedia articles, creating an extremely narrow distribution of training examples that introduces unwanted bias [1][2].
ColBERT is more than 170× faster and requires 14,000× fewer FLOPs per query than existing BERT-based models [1][2].
When used for re-ranking, ColBERT delivers over 170× speedup relative to existing BERT-based models [1]. This speedup is accompanied by a requirement for 14,000× fewer FLOPs [1].
The number of embeddings per query is fixed at Nq = 32 in ColBERT [1].
ColBERT typically uses an embedding dimension of 128 [1][3].
ColBERT prepends the special token [Q] to queries and the special token [D] to documents [3][4].

I do not know. The provided excerpts do not state that the ColBERT document encoder "filters out" any specific content. They only state that the document encoder segments a document into its constituent tokens and prepends BERT's start token [CLS] and a special token [D] [8].

Query augmentation in ColBERT is a step where the padded sequence of input tokens is passed into BERT to produce query-based embeddings at the positions corresponding to masked tokens [1]. This mechanism serves as a soft, differentiable way to learn to expand queries with new terms or re-weigh existing terms based on their importance for matching the query [1]. The ablation results indicate that this operation is essential for ColBERT's effectiveness, as the model without query augmentation achieves a noticeably lower MRR@10 [2][3].

The provided excerpts do not explicitly state the specific faiss index type (e.g., IVF, HNSW) used by ColBERT for end-to-end retrieval. They only mention that ColBERT uses a faiss index, sets the number of partitions to P = 2,000, and searches the nearest p = 10 to each query embedding [2][8].

ColBERT can index the MS MARCO collection in about three hours [1][2].
ColBERT is evaluated on the MS MARCO and TREC CAR (TREC Complex Answer Retrieval) passage search collections [1][7].

The primary difference is that RAG-Sequence uses the same retrieved document to generate the entire output sequence, whereas RAG-Token can draw a different latent document for each individual target token [3][6]. This allows RAG-Token to combine content from several documents when producing an answer, while RAG-Sequence treats the retrieved document as a single latent variable for the whole sequence [2][6].
RAG uses BART-large as its generator, which has 406M parameters [1].
Each Wikipedia article is split into disjoint 100-word chunks, resulting in a total of 21 million documents [1].

The RAG system uses a dense vector index built from a single Wikipedia dump, specifically the December 2018 dump, which is split into disjoint 100-word chunks to create 21 million documents [1]. The retrieval component is based on DPR (Dense Passage Retrieval), which employs a bi-encoder architecture to compute embeddings for documents and queries [8]. During training, the system retrieves the top k documents for each query, with k set to either 5 or 10, while the test time k is selected using development data [1].

In the original RAG model, the parametric memory (a pre-trained seq2seq transformer like BART) and the non-parametric memory (a dense vector index accessed by a pre-trained neural retriever like DPR) are combined in a probabilistic model that is trained end-to-end [2]. This implies that both the retriever and the generator components are fine-tuned during training rather than kept fixed [2]. In contrast, SELF-RAG trains an arbitrary LM to learn to use retrieval on-demand, but the excerpts do not explicitly state whether the retriever itself is fine-tuned or kept fixed in that specific system [4].
In the human evaluation of Jeopardy question generation, RAG was found to be more factual than BART in 42.7% of cases [1][3].

The RAG authors demonstrated index hot-swapping by building an index using the DrQA Wikipedia dump from December 2016 and comparing its outputs to those from a newer index from December 2018 [1]. They specifically prepared a list of 82 world leaders who had changed to illustrate how knowledge can be easily updated at test time without retraining [1].
The compressed RAG document index requires 36GB of CPU memory [1].

Thorough Decoding is a procedure for RAG-Sequence where, to estimate the probability of a hypothesis $y$, an additional forward pass is run for each retrieved document $z$ for which $y$ does not appear in the beam search results [1][6]. The generator probability is then multiplied by the retriever probability $p_\eta(z|x)$, and these probabilities are summed across the beams to compute the marginals [1][6]. This approach is used because the RAG-Sequence likelihood does not break into a conventional per-token likelihood, preventing the use of a single standard beam search [6].
On the FEVER fact verification task, RAG achieves results within 4.3% of state-of-the-art models [1][2][3].
The BEIR benchmark includes 18 datasets and evaluates 10 retrieval systems [5].
BEIR covers nine different retrieval tasks [1][2].
BEIR reports Normalised Cumulative Discount Gain (nDCG@k) as the evaluation metric for all datasets. [1]

The BEIR benchmark concludes that BM25 is a robust and strong baseline for zero-shot text retrieval, often outperforming many neural approaches in generalization despite underperforming them on in-domain tasks like MS MARCO [1][3][7]. While re-ranking and late-interaction models achieve the best average zero-shot performance, they do so at high computational costs, whereas BM25 remains computationally efficient [1][7]. Additionally, the benchmark notes that in-domain performance is not a good indicator for out-of-domain generalization, a fact highlighted by BM25's strong generalization capabilities [3][7].

Re-ranking and late-interaction based models achieve the best zero-shot performance on the BEIR benchmark, but they do so at high computational costs and high latency (over 350 ms) [1][2]. In contrast, dense and sparse-retrieval models are computationally more efficient but often underperform these approaches [1][2].
In the BEIR study, the ColBERT index for BioASQ requires approximately 900GB, whereas the BM25 index requires only 18GB [1][2].

No, according to BEIR, in-domain performance does not predict how well a retrieval model generalizes in a zero-shot setup [1]. The study found that in-domain performance does not correlate well with generalization capabilities, and many approaches that outperform BM25 in-domain perform poorly on the BEIR datasets [1][3].

TAS-B is a bi-encoder model trained with Balanced Topic Aware Sampling using dual supervision from a cross-encoder and a ColBERT model [9]. It utilizes a training setup that combines in-domain batch negatives with Margin-MSE losses and strong ensemble teachers in a Knowledge Distillation setup [6]. This approach allows TAS-B to provide the best zero-shot generalization performance among its dense counterparts, outperforming ANCE on 14 out of 18 datasets and DPR on 17 out of 18 datasets [6].

DocT5query is a document expansion technique that uses a T5 model trained on MS MARCO to generate synthetic queries, which are then appended to the original document to improve lexical search performance [2][4]. It identifies document expansion terms using a sequence-to-sequence model that generates possible queries for which the given document would be relevant [4].

The BEIR authors notice a strong lexical bias in the benchmark datasets, which likely arises because lexical models are predominantly used during the annotation or creation of the datasets [2]. This bias is also described as a selection bias, where candidates for annotation are retrieved using lexical-based systems, causing unseen documents to be automatically assumed irrelevant [1][7].

HyDE stands for Hypothetical Document Embeddings [2]. Its first step is to feed the query to a generative model and instruct it to "write a document that answers the question," creating a hypothetical document [9].

HyDE is implemented using InstructGPT, which is a GPT-3 model from the instruct series (specifically text-davinci-003) [3]. The paper also notes that HyDE can be used with other instruction-following language models, such as the 52-billion Cohere model and the 11-billion FLAN-T5-xxl model [1].

In HyDE, an unsupervised contrastively learned encoder, such as Contriever, turns the hypothetical document into an embedding vector [1][2]. This encoder acts as a lossy compressor or dense bottleneck that filters out incorrect or hallucinated details from the generated document [2][5].
HyDE uses a sampling temperature of 0.7 when generating documents with InstructGPT [1][6].
HyDE is evaluated on Swahili, Korean, Japanese, and Bengali [3][4][8].
The web search query sets used to evaluate HyDE are TREC DL19 and TREC DL20 [8]. These datasets are based on the MS-MARCO dataset [8].

HyDE deals with false details by using an unsupervised contrastively learned encoder to convert the hypothetical document into a dense embedding vector [1]. This encoder acts as a lossy compressor or dense bottleneck that filters out the incorrect or hallucinated details [3][4]. The resulting vector is then used to retrieve similar real documents from the corpus, effectively grounding the generated content to actual data [1][3].
The HyDE retrieval experiments were conducted using the Pyserini toolkit [2].
Besides InstructGPT, HyDE was tested with a 52-billion parameter Cohere model (command-xlarge-20221108) and an 11-billion parameter FLAN model (FLAN-T5-xxl) [1].
HyDE uses the multilingual mContriever model for non-English retrieval tasks. [5]
Ragas measures three quality aspects: faithfulness, answer relevance, and context relevance [1][2].
The RAGAS prompts are evaluated using the gpt-3.5-turbo-16k model, which is available through the OpenAI API [5].
RAGAS uses the text-embedding-ada-002 model, available from the OpenAI API, to compute answer relevance [3].

The RAGAs faithfulness score is computed by first using an LLM to determine whether individual statements in the answer are supported by the context. The final score, F, is then calculated as the ratio of the number of supported statements (|V|) to the total number of statements (|S|), expressed as F = |V| / |S| [3].

The context relevance score is computed as the ratio of the number of extracted sentences to the total number of sentences in the context [3]. Specifically, an LLM extracts a subset of sentences from the context that are crucial for answering the question, and the score is calculated by dividing the count of these extracted sentences by the total sentence count in the provided context [3].

The WikiEval dataset was constructed by selecting 50 Wikipedia pages covering events that occurred since the start of 2022, prioritizing those with recent edits [1][6]. For each page, ChatGPT was used to suggest a question that could be fully answered from the page's introductory section, following specific rules such as ensuring the question contained non-trivial information and was of moderate difficulty [6]. For pages without back-links, ChatGPT was also used to complete the given context [2].
RAGAS provides an integration with LlamaIndex and LangChain [1].
RAGAs achieves an agreement of 0.95 with human annotators on faithfulness [1].
RAGAS is compared against two baseline methods: GPT Score, which asks ChatGPT to assign a score between 0 and 10, and GPT Ranking, which asks ChatGPT to select the preferred answer or context [4][6].
Two human annotators judged the WikiEval questions. [7]

The four types of reflection tokens in Self-RAG are Retrieve, ISREL, ISSUP, and ISUSE [1]. Retrieve determines when to retrieve, ISREL assesses if a passage is relevant, ISSUP evaluates if the output is supported by the passage, and ISUSE rates the usefulness of the response [1].

The training data for the Self-RAG critic model is collected by prompting a proprietary large language model, specifically GPT-4, to generate reflection tokens for input-output pairs [1][4]. This process creates a dataset of inputs, outputs, and corresponding reflection tokens that is used to supervise the critic model [2][4].

The base language model used for the Self-RAG generator is Llama 2-7B [8].
Self-RAG uses the off-the-shelf Contriever-MS MARCO retriever by default [6][7].
Self-RAG was trained using a total of 150k instruction-output pairs [7].
Self-RAG uses a beam width of 2 at each segment level [2].
By default, SELF-RAG sets the retrieval threshold to 0.2 for most tasks, but it sets the threshold to 0 for the ALCE task due to citation requirements [10].

The provided documents do not specify the exact hardware used to train the Self-RAG models, only mentioning that they used DeepSpeed stage 3 for multi-GPU distributed training and ran inference on 1-2 Quadro RTX 6000 GPUs [10].
Self-RAG uses FactScore to evaluate biography generation [3].
Self-RAG is evaluated on two closed-set tasks: a fact verification dataset about public health (PubHealth) and a multiple-choice reasoning dataset created from scientific exams (ARC-C) [7].
